Benjamin Disraeli. The first Prime Minister of Jewish descent and a master of political theatre who transformed the Conservative Party into a vehicle for romantic nationalism and imperial expansion.

Disraeli rose from a background as a novelist and social critic to lead the Conservative Party, embodying the self-made intellectual outsider. He served as Prime Minister twice, first in 1868 and then from 1874 to 1880, using his second term to consolidate Conservative strength and expand British imperial reach.

He famously courted Queen Victoria after Prince Albert's death, positioning himself as her favorite minister and reshaping the Crown's public role. His cultivation of the Queen made him one of the most influential advisors of the Victorian era.

In 1875, Disraeli made the Suez Canal purchase, buying the British government's stake from the debt-ridden Egyptian khedive. This coup of imperial strategy and dramatic political theater secured Britain's waterway to India and captured the public imagination. The following year, he proclaimed Victoria Empress of India, transforming the Crown into a symbol of global dominion that delighted the Queen and magnified British prestige.

Disraeli coined the term "one nation" to describe his vision of a hierarchical but paternalist society united across class divisions. His was a conservatism responsive to working-class needs, a structure of hierarchy married with paternalism and imperial grandeur.
